events.name: The Body Swap

remembers.notice: You know that comet. You heard its Telling: the thing that rides inside it, and how it rearranges whatever it passes. The swap is not a curse. It is a visitor, and visitors can be asked to leave.

success.text: You stand outside at the hour the comet rises and say, out loud, that it can stop now. The sky does a small, polite thing. Your team is back by noon, all of them, blinking. The stranger writes: "It stopped. You did that?" You did. You still know their name, and their handwriting, and the way their Gothita knits its brows. And the Hatenna that crossed over this morning will not let go of your sleeve.

effects.text: You ended the comet's swap on purpose, and kept the stranger's name.

remembers.notice: You know that comet. You heard its Telling: the small wishing star that wakes once in a thousand years and grants things a little too literally. Somebody wished to know what another life was like. A wish can be wished back.

success.text: You wish it back, carefully, in the plainest words you have. The sky does a small, polite thing. Your team is back by noon, all of them, blinking. The stranger writes: "It stopped. You did that?" You did. You still know their name, and their handwriting, and the way their Gothita knits its brows. And the Hatenna that crossed over this morning will not let go of your sleeve.

effects.text: You ended the comet's swap on purpose, and kept the stranger's name.

events.intro: You wake before the sun, and the morning is the wrong shape. The Pokémon curled against your side is not {lead}. It is a Gothita in a hand-knitted scarf, and it is staring at you as if you are the strange one. Your team is gone from the camp. Your phone buzzes: a photo of all of them in a heap on somebody else's bed, across a town you have never seen, while a small pink Hatenna goes from one to the next, patting faces, trying very politely to wake them. A message. "Why is your Pokémon in my bed?" Another. "It's been every third morning. Since the comet." A third. "I left you notes on your hand. Read them." You turn your hand over. There is writing on it, in someone else's careful pen: Don't panic. Feed her at seven. She likes the crusts.

success.text: You type: where are you? The answer takes a long time. Their town is one region ahead of yours, further than you have walked. They send a photo of a crater on the edge of it, rimmed in tall grass, glowing orange. "Dusk is when it thins. If we're both there at dusk, we might get a minute. Maybe only one." You both type "deal" at the same moment. By noon the Gothita blinks out of your arms and {lead} is back, smelling of somebody else's soap.

You borrow a pen and write under their notes, small, so it fits: Hello. Mine like the crusts too. Sorry about the bed. Three mornings on there will be an answer, and three after that another: one useful thing each, the way strangers swap tips on a long road. By noon the Gothita blinks out of your arms and {lead} is back. It sniffs your hand for a long time, reading.

You do nothing, and it stops. One more morning with the Gothita, quieter, then never again. The notes on your hand wash off in the rain. A week later you find yourself writing a name in the margin of your map, and you cannot remember whose it is, or why your chest hurts a little when you look at it.

effects.text: Somebody's name was on your hand once. You cannot work out why it matters.

events.name: Plans for Dusk
events.intro: The third morning again. The Gothita is back, and this time it climbs straight into your lap as if it has been waiting. On your hand, in the careful pen: The crater is on the old road out of town. Bring a light. I will wear something yellow so you know me. Then, smaller, crossed out and written again: I am a bit scared you will be disappointed.

success.text: You draw your side of the road on your own wrist, every bend you can remember, and an arrow that says I will come this way. Your handwriting looks so clumsy next to theirs. By noon the swap ends. A text arrives: "Your map is terrible. I love it." The crater is a region away. It will keep.

"Tall-ish. Hair that does not do what I ask. I laugh too loud." A pause, and then: "You?" You tell them the truth, including the bits you would usually skip. By noon the swap ends. The last message says: "Good. Now I will know you." The crater is a region away. It will keep.

events.name: Notes on Your Hand
events.intro: The third morning again. The Gothita is back, and it hugs your arm before you are properly awake. Your hand is crowded with writing: Your team snores. All of them. In harmony. Your Gym leader here is easy if you know who they open with, so here it is. Under that, a little drawing of the Gothita, with a heart. There is still room on your other hand.

success.text: You write the best thing you know about the road ahead of them: where the berries grow, which bridge is rotten. Then you read their tip properly. It is a good one. It is the exact team the Gym leader keeps, written out in order, with a note about which one bites. By noon the swap ends, and you are smiling at your own hand.

You run out of useful things and write the true one: Thank you for looking after them. Nobody has ever left me notes before. Their tip is still there when the swap ends, the Gym leader's whole team, in order. Three mornings later there is a reply squeezed under your knuckles: Nobody ever wrote back before.

events.name: The Swap Back
events.intro: The comet is low tonight, low enough to see it moving. This is the last swap morning: you can feel it the way you feel the end of a fever. But this time it is not the Gothita in your arms. It is the Hatenna, the little pink one that kept trying to wake your team. It crossed over with them, on purpose it seems, and it is holding on to your scarf with both hands. Your phone buzzes. "Is she with you? She has sat by your Pokémon every morning. I think she likes your side better." Then: "Still the crater? Still dusk?"

success.text: It does not let go. When the swap ends at noon and your team blinks back into the camp, the Hatenna is still in your arms, small and warm and very sure. Your phone buzzes. "I think it chose you. It always did like the snoring." Then: "Look after it. I will know if you don't. I have your hand, sometimes."

effects.text: Every third morning you lived beside a stranger's life. Their Hatenna stayed.

choices.label: Send it home with the comet.

success.text: You hold it until the last minute and then you set it down where the swap will take it. It looks back at you once. At noon your team is home, and a message arrives: "She came back holding your scarf. Thank you. See you at the crater." The comet goes, and the mornings are only mornings again.

events.name: The Last Note
events.intro: The comet is low tonight, low enough to see it moving. This is the last swap morning: you can feel it the way you feel the end of a fever. But this time it is not the Gothita in your arms. It is the Hatenna, the little pink one that kept trying to wake your team. It crossed over with them, on purpose it seems, and it is holding on to your scarf with both hands. One last note runs up the inside of your wrist: The comet goes tonight. This is the last one. Tip: the road ahead forks three times, and here is what waits down each. I will miss your handwriting. It is terrible.

success.text: It does not let go. When the swap ends at noon and your team blinks back into the camp, the Hatenna is still in your arms, small and warm and very sure. Your phone buzzes. "I think it chose you. It always did like the snoring." Then: "Look after it. I will know if you don't. I have your hand, sometimes."

effects.text: Every third morning you lived beside a stranger's life. Their Hatenna stayed.

choices.label: Send it home with the comet.

success.text: You hold it until the last minute and then you set it down where the swap will take it. It looks back at you once. At noon your team is home, and a message arrives: "She came back holding your scarf. Thank you." It is the last message. The tip is still on your wrist, and you do not wash it off for days.

effects.text: Every third morning you lived beside a stranger's life. You sent their Hatenna home.

events.name: A Crater at Dusk
events.intro: The old road. The crater, exactly like the photo, only bigger and more orange, because the sun is going down into it. You are early. You walk the rim twice. Then, on the far side, something yellow, running. The air goes thin and strange as dusk thickens: this is where the swap wears through, and you can feel it pulling at the edges of you. A minute. Maybe only one. The yellow figure is waving both arms.

success.text: You shout it across the crater, the whole thing, and it comes back to you from the far side in their voice, shouted just as loud, as if they are checking they have it right. Then they shout theirs. You say it under your breath three times so it sticks. The light goes. The minute is over. You are both still waving when you can no longer see each other.

effects.text: At a crater at dusk you finally saw the stranger whose mornings you shared. You know their name.

success.text: You run along the rim and they run along the rim, and you get close enough to see that their hair really does not do what they ask. Close enough to touch hands, almost. Their hand has your handwriting on it. Yours has theirs. Then the dusk closes like a door and there is only grass and the sound of someone laughing too loud, far off, happy.

effects.text: At a crater at dusk you ran to meet a stranger whose mornings you shared, and nearly touched hands.

events.name: The Quiet Psychic
events.intro: A small cafe, warm and steamy, and very quiet, because every spoon in it is floating. They hang over the tables at about eye height, turning slowly, catching the light. The other customers are pretending not to notice. In the corner a boy in a school uniform has both hands pressed flat on the table and his eyes shut. "Sorry," he says, to nobody, to everybody. "That happens when I'm nervous." He opens one eye and finds you looking. "I'm trying to join the running club. I want to be good at something normal." His Gothita sighs, climbs onto the table, and floats the spoons back to their saucers, one by one, with a tiny clink each time.

success.text: You race him to the end of the street and back. He runs like someone who has read about running in a book: elbows everywhere, very determined. He loses by a long way. He bends over with his hands on his knees, gasping, and when he looks up he is grinning so hard it must hurt. "I lost! I lost properly! Nothing floated!" The Gothita applauds with two small hands. "The tryout is soon. Will you come?"

choices.label: Show me what you can do.

success.text: He looks at you for a long moment. Then he lifts one finger, and every cup in the cafe rises an inch and settles again, without spilling a drop. It is beautiful. It is also the moment the door bangs open.

He laughs, sudden and loud, and three spoons leap into the air and fall back down. "Says you." He wipes his eyes. "You get to be normal and you're bored of it. I'd like to be bored of it." The Gothita pats his hand. "The tryout is soon. You could come and be overrated in the stands."

events.name: If I Get Angry
events.intro: Two grunts of the team that has been trouble all region, in matching jackets, too big for the doorway. "Heard there was a kid in here doing tricks," one says. "The boss pays for tricks." The boy has gone white. The cups on every table start to tremble, and then the tables, and then the windows. "Please go," he whispers. "I don't know what I'll do if I get angry. I've never let myself find out." His Gothita has both hands on his arm, holding on.

success.text: You step between the grunts and the boy. Behind you, the trembling slows. He is watching you instead of them.

You sit down across from him and breathe in for four, out for four, and make him copy you. In. Out. The grunts laugh. The windows stop rattling. Then the Gothita, very calmly, floats both grunts out of the door by their collars and sets them down in the road. Nobody got angry. The boy stares at his hands. "I didn't do that." "No," you say. "You did the other thing. The harder one."

failure.text: You try to get him breathing, but he is already too far in. Every spoon in the cafe flies at the door at once. They do not hit anyone; they hang there, an inch from the grunts' faces, quivering. The grunts run. The boy puts his head in his arms. "That's what I'm scared of. That's exactly it." His Gothita strokes his hair until he stops shaking.

events.name: The Running Club

remembers.notice: At the back of the stands sits a man in a grey-and-silver coat with a clipboard. He is not watching the runners. He is watching the boy, and the hurdles that wobble when the boy is nervous. He writes something down and underlines it twice.

At the back of the stands sits a man in a long robe with a clipboard. He is not watching the runners. He is watching the boy, and the hurdles that wobble when the boy is nervous. He writes something down and underlines it twice.

events.intro: The school track, chalk lines and a whistle. The running club tryout. The boy is in borrowed shorts, much too big. He keeps looking at the hurdles as if they might float off without him. "If they float, I'm out," he says. "If I'm last, that's fine. Last is a normal thing to be." His Gothita is in the stands with its hands over its eyes, peeking.

success.text: You shout his name every time he gets near a hurdle. He knocks over the first one, clears the second, and walks round the third out of politeness. He finishes dead last, by a mile, and every hurdle on the track stays exactly where it was. He walks back to you with his arms up like a champion. "Last! Did you see? Nothing moved!" The coach writes his name on the list anyway: for trying harder than anyone.

You run in the next lane, matching him stride for stride, and count the hurdles out loud so he has something to think about besides being afraid. One. Two. Three. You both clear every one. He finishes second to last, and the boy behind him is a very small first-year who tripped over his own lace, but it still counts. He cannot stop laughing.

failure.text: You lose the count on the second hurdle and go down in a heap, and he stops to help you up, and you both finish last together, limping and laughing. Nothing floated. Not even when you fell. The coach writes his name on the list: for stopping.

events.name: His Mother's Gothitelle

remembers.notice: There is a knock. On the step stands the man with the clipboard, in grey and silver, and two grunts behind him. "We take gifted children seriously," he says. "He is next on our list." The boy's cups begin to tremble. You are standing in the doorway before you have decided to.

success.text: The boy is behind you. His breathing is steady. In, four. Out, four.

win.text: A team came to take a gifted boy, and you stood in the door.

lose.text: A team came to take a gifted boy. He stayed calm, and they left.

remembers.notice: There is a knock. On the step stands the man with the clipboard, in a long robe, and two grunts behind him. "Such power should be set free," he says. "He is next on our list." The boy's cups begin to tremble. You are standing in the doorway before you have decided to.

success.text: The boy is behind you. His breathing is steady. In, four. Out, four.

win.text: A team came to take a gifted boy, and you stood in the door.

lose.text: A team came to take a gifted boy. He stayed calm, and they left.

events.intro: The boy's house is small and very tidy, with a kettle that boils without being switched on. His mother meets you at the door. Behind her stands a Gothitelle, tall and calm, with something cradled in its arms: an egg, faintly starry. "He told me about you," his mother says. "He has never brought anyone home." Her Gothitelle steps forward and holds the egg out to you, the way you would hand someone a cup of tea. "She wants you to have it. She decided before we did."

success.text: It is warm, and it hums a little against your chest. The boy is grinning at the floor. "It'll be nervous too. When it hatches. Things might float." He shrugs. "That's normal." His mother laughs so suddenly that every spoon in the kitchen jumps, and nobody minds at all.

effects.text: A boy who wanted to be normal finished last, and was delighted. His mother's Gothitelle gave you an egg.

choices.label: Say it should stay with him.

success.text: "He'll need someone who understands," you say. The Gothitelle tilts its head, and then sets the egg in the boy's arms instead. He holds it as if it might float away. "I'll teach it to run," he says. "Badly. Like me." He walks you to the gate and waves until you turn the corner.

events.name: The Bounty Crew

remembers.notice: The captain squints at you, and his face changes. "Wait. You're the one who broke the Smuggling Ring. Del, it's them!" The woman at the rail looks up. "Then you know him already," she says. "The man on the poster ran that ring. He got out the back while you were opening cages."

events.intro: A boat at the end of the jetty that should have sunk years ago. The paint is mostly rust, the rust is mostly hope. On deck: a big man in a battered captain's hat, a woman sharpening a knife at the rail with a Barraskewda circling below her, an old man asleep under a newspaper with a Cramorant asleep on top of him, and a Yamper with one ear up, guarding a pot with nothing in it. "We hunt bounties," says the captain, Rufus Kettleby. "We're bad at it." He unrolls a poster. "This one's worth a fortune. A trainer who sells stolen Pokémon." He taps the face. "Help us catch him and we split it."

success.text: "IN!" Kettleby throws his hat in the air and it lands in the sea. The Yamper goes in after it. The old man wakes up and says, "Is it dinner?" It is not dinner. Del watches you over her knife and says nothing at all. "Three ports on," the captain says, dripping, holding his hat. "That's where he sells. We'll be waiting."

Nobody answers. The captain looks at his boots. The old man pretends to be asleep again. Then the woman at the rail puts down her knife. "Corwin Arkwright," Del says. "He sells stolen Pokémon to people who don't ask. He used to carry me on his shoulders." She picks the knife up again. "He's my brother. I'd rather it was us that caught him than anyone else."

"Fair," says the captain, cheerfully, as if nobody has ever said yes. "More for us. Which is nothing, currently." The Yamper sees you off down the jetty, very seriously, and then trots back to guard the empty pot.

events.name: His Sister
events.intro: Del does not look at you while she talks. "Our dad fished. Corwin took over the boat when he died, and then he sold the boat, and then he sold other things." Below her, the Barraskewda turns a slow circle. "If someone else catches him, they won't be careful. I will be." The captain clears his throat. "The offer stands. Same split. Five ways, dog included."

success.text: Del nods, once, the way people nod when they have been carrying something alone and somebody finally takes the other end. "Three ports on," the captain says. "That's where he sells. We'll be waiting." The old man wakes up and asks if it is dinner. It is not.
"Fair," the captain says, quieter this time. Del goes back to her knife. As you leave you hear her say, to the Barraskewda or to nobody, "Then it's us." The Yamper sees you down the jetty.

events.name: The Chase
events.intro: The third port, at dusk, in the rain. Corwin Arkwright is exactly where the poster said: on the end of a pier, selling a crate of frightened Pokémon to a man with a thick wallet. Kettleby charges up the pier shouting "BOUNTY HUNTERS!", which is the one thing you agreed not to do. Corwin is in a speedboat before the captain finishes the word. The engine coughs, roars, and he is away across the harbour.

success.text: You and Del race the long way round the harbour wall while the Barraskewda shoots through the water like a thrown spear. You get close enough to see his face: he looks like Del, older, tired. Then he cuts the engine, drifts into the fog under the old pier and is gone. He escaped. The crate is still on the pier, and it is open now. Every Pokémon in it is free.

You leave the captain shouting and follow the wake in a rowing boat, quietly, the old man rowing with surprising strength. You see where the speedboat ties up: a dock with a red lamp. Then the captain's voice carries across the water, still shouting, and the red lamp goes out. He escaped. But you know where he sleeps now.

events.name: The Argument About Dinner
events.intro: Back on the boat, nobody is talking about Corwin. Everybody is talking about dinner. There is one onion, a tin of something with no label, and the old man's Cramorant, which has a fish in its throat it will not give up. The captain wants to sell the tin. The old man wants to open it. The Yamper wants the fish. Del sits at the rail and does not want anything. "We eat or we chase," the captain says. "We can't afford both."

success.text: You open the tin (beans), chop the onion, and coax the fish out of the Cramorant with a pat on the back. It is not a good dinner. Everybody has two helpings. The Yamper falls asleep in the pot. Halfway through, Del says, "He used to cook for me. Badly. Like this." And she laughs, and then she cries a bit, and the captain passes her the last of the beans without a word.

You leave them arguing and sit at the rail. Del does not look at you. "When we catch him," she says, "I want to be the one who tells him." Behind you, the captain wins the argument by eating the tin cold. The Cramorant keeps its fish. Nobody gets much dinner, and nobody minds.

events.name: The Catch
events.intro: The dock with the red lamp, before dawn. Corwin Arkwright is loading his last crate. He turns, sees the crew, sees Del, and goes very still. "Delly," he says. "You got old." "You got worse," she says. He looks past her, at you. "Who's this? The muscle?" His hand goes to his belt, where his Poké Balls are. "I'm not going quietly, Delly. I don't know how."

success.text: Del stands at your shoulder. The captain, for once, is silent.

You step back. Del walks up to her brother and stands in front of him for a long time. She says something too quiet for anyone else. He sits down on his last crate. He gives her his Poké Balls, one by one, the stolen ones. Then he holds out his wrists. The captain, who was ready to shout, takes off his hat instead.

events.name: Payday
events.intro: The bounty office pays out in a paper bag. Kettleby counts it on the deck, twice, out loud. "Six thousand. Five ways: me, Del, the old man, the dog, you. Twelve hundred each. That's honest." The dog's share goes straight into a new pot. Del has not touched hers. The Barraskewda in the water below her has had a baby since you last looked: a small Arrokuda, all teeth and nerves, darting round your boots. "It likes you," says Del. "Take it. He'd have sold it."

success.text: Twelve hundred, honest, in a paper bag that smells of fish. The little Arrokuda jumps into your arms as if it has been practising. "Same time next bounty?" the captain says. "We'll be bad at it again." Del walks you to the end of the jetty. "Thank you for being careful with him," she says, and goes back aboard.

effects.text: You rode with a broke bounty crew and helped a woman bring her brother in, carefully.

success.text: You put your twelve hundred on top of hers. "For his lawyer," you say. "Or for you." She stares at the money, and then at you, and then she has to look at the sea for a while. The little Arrokuda jumps into your arms anyway. "Still broke," the captain announces happily. "Still a crew."

effects.text: You rode with a broke bounty crew, and gave your share of the bounty to the hunter whose brother it was.

events.name: Caught by Accident
events.intro: A rusty boat comes past the harbour wall, very slowly, with a speedboat tied to its back. On the speedboat sits a man in handcuffs, looking furious. On the rusty boat, Captain Kettleby is waving his hat at you with both arms. "WE GOT HIM! Total accident! He ran out of fuel and drifted into us while we were fishing!" The Yamper barks. The old man is asleep. Del, at the rail, raises one hand to you, calmly, the way you raise a hand at the end of something.

success.text: "Six thousand!" the captain bellows. "We're rich! For a week!" The boat goes past, and as it does the Yamper drops something over the side onto the jetty at your feet: a small Arrokuda in a bucket of water, all teeth and nerves. "SPARE ONE!" the captain shouts. "DON'T ASK!" You did not help. You get no cut. You get a fish with opinions.
The boat goes past, shouting. You do not need to hear the end of it to know how it goes. They will be broke again by Tuesday.

events.name: The Forest God

remembers.notice: Deep in the trees, a green light flickers, then another: the same small lights you gathered across this run, the Cells. The forest groans again, and this time it sounds like a name. Yours. The girl turns and stares at you. "It knows you," she says. "It never knows anyone."

addChoices.label: Let the forest speak for itself.

success.text: You walk into the trees and the green lights come with you, and the foreman, swearing, comes too. The forest shows him: every dead trunk lights up green, one by one, the whole way to the hill. He stands there with his hat in his hands. "That's enough wood for three winters," he says. "And not one living tree." The girl looks at you as if you have done magic. You have only been kind to some small green lights.

events.intro: The edge of an old forest, and a line of stumps where the trees used to stop. Loggers are packing up for the night. In the morning, they say, every stump they cut has grown a face: a small, sad, wooden face, with a single leaf on top. Some of the faces have started to cry. The foreman wipes his hands on his trousers. "It's just a forest. We need the wood." From the trees, where something huge and dark stands among the trunks, comes a groan so deep you feel it in your teeth: a Trevenant, and the whole forest groaning with it, one sound. Then a girl steps out of the dark between the trunks, barefoot, with a Phantump on her shoulder. "Leave," she says, "or I'll make you."

success.text: You stand between the saws and the trees. The girl, behind you, says nothing. The forest is very quiet, listening.

He is not a cruel man. He is a tired one. "Town's got no coal this year. Kids need heat." He looks at the stumps with their little faces and has to look away. "Dead wood burns as well as live. I'd cut only dead, if someone could show me which. I can't tell. It all looks alive to me now." He sticks out his hand. "Come back when the crew's ready. Show us."

She looks at you for a long time, the way a wild thing does before it decides whether to run. The Phantump on her shoulder makes a small, creaking sound. "Fine," she says. "You can meet it. If it wants to meet you." She turns into the trees. "It's a long walk. Don't talk too much."

events.name: No Wood for Winter
events.intro: The town below the forest. The first frost has come. The woodpiles behind the houses are empty, and smoke rises from only a few chimneys, thin and grudging. The foreman is at his door with a child on his hip, both of them in coats indoors. He sees you and does not look angry. That is worse. "You saved the trees," he says. "Good. Who's saving us?" Behind him, the child's breath shows in the air.

choices.label: Cut the dead wood with them.

success.text: You go back up with the crew and you show them, trunk by trunk, which trees are already dead: the hollow ones, the lightning-struck, the ones with no sap. It is slow, cold work. The forest watches. It does not groan. By dark there is a cart of dry wood going down the hill, and that night more chimneys smoke. The foreman shakes your hand without a word.

You do not offer anything. It is the forest or the town, and you chose. You walk through the cold streets and nobody shouts at you, which is somehow the hard part. A girl at a window has drawn a tree in the frost on the glass. It has a face. That night you lie awake listening to the wind in a forest that will stand for another hundred years.

events.name: Which Wood Is Dead
events.intro: The crew is ready, saws on shoulders, standing at the edge of the trees like men at the door of a church. The foreman hands you a pot of white paint. "Mark the dead ones. We'll cut nothing else." Somewhere in the forest the girl is watching, you are sure of it. A Phantump peers at you from behind a trunk. Every tree looks alive in this light. Every tree looks like it has a face.

choices.label: Let a Pokémon find the dead wood.

success.text: Your Pokémon goes ahead of you, sniffing, listening, laying a paw or a leaf against each trunk. Where it stops and sits, you paint a white ring. It never stops at a living tree. By evening the crew has felled only the dead, and the forest has not groaned once. The foreman gives your Pokémon an apple. The girl, somewhere above you, laughs out loud.

You walk the forest with the paint pot and look properly: at bark, at leaves, at the sap that still runs and the trunks that ring hollow when you knock. You get them right, every one. By dark the crew has felled only the dead. The foreman looks at the stumps. Not one of them has a face.

failure.text: You get almost all of them right. Almost. In the morning one stump at the edge of the clearing has grown a small, sad face, with one leaf on top, and it is looking straight at you. The foreman swears softly. The forest groans, once, long. You did your best. It was not quite enough, and everybody knows it.

events.name: The Forest God
events.intro: The middle of the forest, where the light comes down green. The girl stops. "Here." At first you think it is a hill. Then the hill opens its eye: a single red eye, the size of a doorway. It is a Trevenant, but older and bigger than any Trevenant should be, with whole trees growing out of its back and a stream running between its roots. The girl kneels. "This is who raised me," she says. "It doesn't like people. It's deciding about you."

success.text: You sit down in the moss and say nothing. For a long time, nothing happens. Then the forest god groans, and the girl translates, slowly, as if the words are heavy. "It says the town may have the dead. It says the living are its children. It says one tree planted for every tree cut, and a line nobody crosses." She looks at you. "It wants you to carry that to them. It thinks they'll listen to you."

choices.label: Ask it to spare the town.

success.text: "They're cold," you say. "They're not cruel. They're cold." The red eye looks at you for so long that your legs go numb. Then a branch the size of a bridge lowers itself, slowly, and sets down a heap of dry, dead wood at your feet. Then another. The girl's mouth is open. "It's never given anything," she whispers. "Not to them."

events.name: The Border

remembers.notice: The loggers remember the fight. The forest remembers that you stood in front of it. Neither side has forgotten the cold.
The stumps along the line are all dead wood, cut clean. The foreman has painted a white ring on a stone, the same white you used.
Behind the girl, half hidden in the trees, a hill with a single red eye is watching.

events.intro: A cold bright morning at the edge of the forest. The foreman is there with his crew, and the girl with her Phantump, and they are not shouting at each other. They are carrying stones. They have been arguing all week about where the line goes, and they have asked you to settle it, because you are the only one both sides have talked to. A row of stones runs half way across the field and stops. "Here, or there?" the foreman says. "Wherever you put it," says the girl, "we keep it. Both sides."

choices.label: Draw it at the old stumps.

success.text: You set the last stone at the line of old stumps, where the trees used to stop before anyone was cold. The foreman nods slowly. The girl nods slowly. They shake hands, which neither expected. One of the little faced stumps creaks, wriggles, and climbs out of the ground: a Phantump, all leaf and worry. It walks straight past the girl and holds on to your leg. "It wants to see the world," she says. "Trees never get to."

effects.text: You drew the border between a town and a forest god, and both sides kept it.

success.text: You carry the stones up to the hill and set the line above the town, so the forest keeps its old ground and the town keeps its fields. It costs the crew a long walk for wood. The foreman grumbles and agrees. The girl looks at you as if she might cry. A Phantump climbs out of a stump at your feet and wraps itself round your ankle. "That one's yours," she says. "It chose. Look after it."

effects.text: You drew the border between a town and a forest god, and gave the forest its hill.

events.name: The Descent
events.intro: A pit in the ground, round as a well and wide as a village, so deep that the light gives up a little way down and simply stops. Cold air breathes out of it, slow, like something asleep. A girl sits on the rim with her boots laced tight and a lamp on her pack. In her hand is an envelope gone soft with folding. "My mum went down years ago," she says. "She sent one letter back." She holds it up. "It says come down. So I'm going." A Clodsire is lying across the top of the path, broad and calm, blocking the way. It looks at the girl for a long time. Then it heaves itself aside. "Going up is the hard part," the girl says. "Everyone says that."

success.text: She looks at you as if nobody has ever said that to her before. Then she hands you the other end of her rope. "Don't let go unless I say." The Clodsire watches you both step over the edge.

You sit beside her on the rim and talk about anything else until it gets dark: the towns ahead, her Pokémon, what her mum was like. She listens. She nods. She says, "You're right. Tomorrow." You believe her. That night you wake to the sound of a rope paying out over stone.

She hands it over without a word. The paper is old, soft as cloth, and the handwriting shakes: big loops that wander off the lines and come back. Only two words are steady, near the bottom, pressed so hard they nearly went through the page.

events.name: The Letter
events.intro: "My darling. It is more beautiful down here than I can write. The air is warm on the fourth floor. There are little walking mushrooms that sing. I am well. I am mostly well. Come down." The last two words are the steady ones. The girl watches you read. "Her writing used to be neat," she says, quietly. "She was a teacher. I know what the shaking means. I'm going anyway."

success.text: You fold the letter carefully along its old lines and give it back. She puts it inside her coat, over her heart. Then she hands you the other end of her rope. "Don't let go unless I say."

You give the letter back. She nods as if she expected it, ties her rope to the post, and goes over the edge without looking back. The lamp on her pack gets smaller and smaller, and then the dark has it. The Clodsire lies down across the path again.

events.name: At Night, Alone
events.intro: Moonlight on the rim. The girl's rope is tied to the old post and running down into the pit, still moving. Far below, so small it could be a star, her lamp. She did not say goodbye. The Clodsire is sitting at the top of the rope, looking down, and then it looks at you, and back at the rope, as if to say: well?

success.text: You climb down after her, fast, faster than is sensible. Two floors down you catch up. She is sitting on a ledge, crying a little, not because she is hurt. "I didn't want you to say no again," she says. You give her your hand, and she takes it, and you go on together.

You sit by the rope until it stops moving. The Clodsire sits with you. Neither of you sleeps. In the morning the rope is still there, tied to the post, going down into the dark, and you leave it exactly as it is, in case she needs it.

events.name: The First Floor
events.intro: Down is easy. That is the first surprise. The path spirals gently round the inside of the pit, wide and dry, and the walls are covered in a soft moss that glows blue-green when you touch it. The girl touches all of it. Her hand-prints glow behind her like a trail. "She came this way," she says. "I can feel it. She would have touched everything too."

success.text: You go on. Your feet find the way without trying. Behind you the glowing hand-prints fade, slowly, one by one.

choices.label: Leave a mark for the way back.

success.text: You press your whole hand flat on the moss and hold it there until it glows bright as a lamp. The girl does the same beside it: two hands, side by side. "So we know which way is up," she says. You go on, down, and it is still easy.

events.name: The Second Floor
events.intro: Warmer. The air smells of wet stone and something sweet. You hear a heavy, comfortable sound behind you: the Clodsire from the rim, coming down the path at its own pace. It has followed you. It walks past you both, and on the next bend it stops beside a wall where someone has scratched words into the stone, a long time ago. Floor two. Still fine. Still beautiful. The handwriting is steady here. The girl puts her fingers in the letters.

success.text: She traces the words one more time, the way you would touch somebody's sleeve. Then she goes on, faster now. The Clodsire comes too.

events.name: The Third Floor
events.intro: The third floor is a forest of pale stalks, taller than you, gently swaying though there is no wind. Things move between them: small, flat, frilled, on many little legs. Toedscool, dozens of them, walking about their business in the dark like a town at evening. There is another message scratched in the stone. Floor three. My hands are not good today. Still beautiful. The letters wander. The girl reads it twice and does not say anything.

success.text: You go on, down through the swaying stalks. The Toedscool part to let you through and close again behind you. One of them follows a little way, curious, and then a little further.

You do not say anything either. You just take her hand. She grips it so hard it hurts, and keeps hold of it all the way down to the fourth floor. A Toedscool follows the two of you the whole way, as if it is keeping you company.

events.name: The Bottom
events.intro: The fourth floor. The bottom. It is warm, as the letter said, and it is beautiful: a wide cave of glowing moss and pale stalks, and everywhere the soft singing of the Toedscool colony, hundreds of them, humming to each other in the dark. In the middle, by an old fire ring, is a camp. A tent, neatly folded. A cup. A blanket. Nobody. On the folded tent lies an envelope, with the girl's name on the front in big, shaking loops.

success.text: She opens it with her back to you. You do not read it. You only hear her breathe in, once, and then she laughs, wetly. "She says she went further. Down where it's quiet. She says not to follow. She says go up slowly, and that she's proud of me for coming." She folds it into her coat beside the first. The Toedscool that followed you down is sitting on your boot. It does not intend to get off.

"I can't," she says, and gives it to you. You read it aloud. My darling. If you are reading this, you came down, and I am so proud and so angry. I have gone further, where it is quiet. Do not follow. Go up slowly. Up is the brave part. I love you. You fold it. She takes it. The little Toedscool on your boot hums, very softly, all the way through.

events.name: Going Up

remembers.notice: Your Ground- or Poison-type, the one closest to you, goes first. It knows this kind of dark. It finds the footholds, tests them, waits for you. The weight on your back is still there, but only half of it.

success.text: You put your feet where your partner puts its feet. It is still hard. It is only half as hard. On the ledge at the top of the floor, the girl sits down and looks back at the light of the colony, far below, and does not cry.

events.intro: Up is the hard part. Everyone said so, and everyone was right. The path that ran so easily down now leans against you. Every step pulls, as if the pit wants its visitors back. Your legs are heavy. Your Pokémon are heavy. The girl stops at the first bend, out of breath already. "It's the curse," she whispers. "Mum wrote about it. Each floor up, it takes a bit of you." The Clodsire is waiting on the path above, patient as a stone.

success.text: You climb. It takes something from every one of you, a little, the way a long day does. At the top of the floor you all sit on the ledge in a heap, breathing, and the Clodsire waits until you are ready.

You take her pack on top of yours. It is heavier than it looks: two letters, a lamp and a whole childhood. The pit takes more of you for it. At the top of the floor she says, "Thanks," very small, and holds your sleeve.

events.name: Through the Stalks

remembers.notice: Your partner leads you through the pale stalks without a wrong turn. The pull is there, but it takes only half of what it takes from anyone else.

success.text: Step where it steps. The Toedscool colony hums behind you, softer and softer, until it is only a feeling. At the top of the floor the girl looks back once, down into the glow, and then she does not look back again.

events.intro: The third floor again, from below: the forest of pale stalks, swaying, and the Toedscool going about their evening. The words on the wall: Floor three. My hands are not good today. Still beautiful. Going down, they frightened you. Going up, they are the bravest thing you have ever read. The pull is stronger now. The girl stops and leans her forehead on the stone beside them, just for a moment.

success.text: You climb. The pit takes its share again, a little from every one of you. The little Toedscool that joined you rides on your pack, humming, as if to say this is nothing.

You take her pack. She lets you this time without arguing. The pit takes more of you for it. At the top of the floor she says, "She did this with bad hands. Every day." Then, "I can do it with good ones."

events.name: Further Up

remembers.notice: Your partner goes first again, steady, finding the footholds in the dark. You climb in its tracks, and the pull of the pit is only half as strong.

success.text: Step where it steps. Breathe when it breathes. You pass the old words scratched in the wall, Floor two, still fine, and the girl touches them on the way up, too.

events.intro: The second floor again, from below. The words on the wall: Floor two. Still fine. Still beautiful. They looked hopeful going down. Coming up, they look brave. The pit pulls harder here. The girl's lamp swings and she stops to catch her breath. "Two more," she says. "Two more. She did this every day for a year. Up and down."

success.text: You climb. Your Pokémon climb. The pit takes its share again, a little more from everyone. At the top of the floor you lie flat on your back and look up, and there, very far away, is a circle of grey that might be sky.

You take her pack again. She tries to argue, and gives up halfway through, too tired. The pit takes more from you for it. She walks the next bend holding the end of the rope as if you were towing her home.

events.name: Nearly Up

remembers.notice: Your partner does not even look back now. It knows you will follow. It climbs, and you climb, and the pull of the pit is only half of what it is for anyone else.

success.text: One more floor at your partner's pace. The glowing hand-prints on the first floor are long faded, but the moss lights up again as you pass, as if it remembers you.

events.intro: The first floor. The moss still glows where you touch it. The air is cold again, and it smells, faintly, of grass. The pull is worst here, right at the end, as if the pit is making one last argument. The girl's legs are shaking. So are yours. Above, the circle of grey is bigger. It is sky. It is definitely sky.

success.text: The last floor takes the most, and you give it. Every one of you. Then a hand reaches down from the rim, broad and grey and damp: the Clodsire's, or the Clodsire itself, leaning over. You grab hold. It hauls.
You carry it the whole last floor. You do not think you will make it, and then you do. The Clodsire is leaning over the rim, and it hauls you both up into the cold air as if you weigh nothing at all.

events.name: The List of Those Who Came Back
events.intro: Daylight. Real, ordinary, enormous daylight. You lie in the grass at the rim of the pit and cannot get up for a while. Nobody can. Then the girl sits up and points. Beside the old post, under a little roof against the rain, is a board. It is covered in names: some carved, some painted, some scratched with a stone. A sign over it says: THESE CAME BACK. There is room at the bottom. The girl holds out the pen she brought to write to her mother.

choices.label: Let her write her own name.

success.text: She writes it slowly, in neat, careful, steady letters, the way her mother used to write. She looks at it for a long time. "She'll see it," she says, "if she ever comes up." Then she writes, underneath, smaller: and a friend. The Clodsire lies down across the path again, exactly where it was, as if it is waiting for somebody else.

effects.text: You went down into the pit with a girl looking for her mother, and climbed back up. Her name is on the list of those who came back.

success.text: You write yours and she writes hers, side by side, the way your hands glowed side by side on the moss. She leans on you, worn out, and laughs, and the laugh echoes down into the pit a long, long way. Somewhere at the bottom, maybe, somebody hears it. The Clodsire lies down across the path again, waiting for somebody else.

effects.text: You went down into the pit with a girl looking for her mother, and climbed back up. Both your names are on the list of those who came back.

events.name: The Sword of the Insect
events.intro: Night, on a road through tall grass. A boy not much older than a child is walking it with a short sword at his hip, in a sheath mended with tape. He moves the way hunters move: quiet, looking at the dark instead of the road. Behind him, a little above his shoulder, something hovers. A Shedinja: a hollow shell, brown and gold, with a halo, and a crack down its back where nothing lives. It makes no sound. It does not blink. It follows him exactly. "She's a Shedinja now," the boy says, without turning round. "She doesn't eat. She doesn't age. She follows me." He puts his hand on the sword. "Someone made her that way. I'm hunting them."

success.text: He looks at you properly for the first time. Then he nods, once, a grown-up nod on a young face. "They come out at night. They move a machine on a cart. I've found its tracks." He shows you: two deep ruts in the mud, and around them, shed Nincada skins, dozens, all split down the back. "Three nights," he says. "Then I'll have them." The Shedinja hangs in the air, listening, or not.

He is quiet for a long time. The Shedinja turns slowly in the air, as if the question has a draught in it. "I don't know," he says at last. "I'm going to find out." He says it the way you would set down something heavy and pick it up again in the same breath.

He hesitates. Then he steps aside. The Shedinja drifts forward until it is in front of you, very close, and stops. It does not move. It does not look at you, because it has no eyes to look with, but you are certain it is waiting for something. "She does this," the boy says. "With everyone. She waits for them to tell her who she is."

events.name: Not Knowing
events.intro: The boy sits down on a milestone and takes the sword off and lays it across his knees. "Everyone wants to know if she can be changed back. Doctors. Professors. A woman at a Pokémon Center cried." He looks up at the shell above his head. "The one who did it will know. That's why I'm hunting them. Not to hurt them." A pause. "Maybe a bit to hurt them."

success.text: "Three nights," he says, standing up, putting the sword back on. "They come out at night and move a machine on a cart." He shows you the ruts in the mud and the split Nincada skins around them. "Then I'll know." The Shedinja follows him exactly.

"Fair," he says. He puts the sword back on, and walks off into the grass the way he came, quiet, looking at the dark. The Shedinja follows him exactly, a little above his shoulder. It does not look back. It has no way to.

events.name: Who She Is

remembers.notice: You have stood in front of a shell like this before, at three rests, and answered it. Maybe she can tell. She does not wait this time. She turns in the air, once, all the way round, the way a person turns in a new coat. Then she settles beside the boy's shoulder, where she always is.

success.text: You say nothing at all, and that turns out to be right. She drifts back to the boy and taps the crack in her own shell against his cheek, very gently. He goes completely still. "She's never done that," he whispers. She stays a Shedinja. She is not sad about it. Somehow, now, neither is he. "Will you help me find them anyway?" he asks. "Not to change her. To stop them doing it to anyone else."

events.intro: The Shedinja hangs in front of you. Up close, the shell is beautiful: gold at the edges, thin as paper, with the light coming through the crack in its back. There is nothing inside. There is somebody inside. The boy holds his breath. Whatever you tell her, he will hear it too.

success.text: The shell does not move for a long time. Then it drifts back, slowly, to the place above his shoulder, and stays there, a little closer than before. The boy rubs his eyes hard with the heel of his hand. "Thanks," he says, rough. "Nobody ever says that to her. They say it."

It is true, and she seems to take it as true. She turns once, slowly, as if trying the word on. The boy says nothing. Then she drifts back to him and settles above his shoulder, exactly where she was. A Shedinja that follows her brother is still a girl who follows her brother.

choices.label: You're whoever you decide to be.

success.text: That one takes the longest. She hangs there in the dark, perfectly still, and you cannot tell if she understood. Then she rises, higher than she has ever gone, high enough to catch the moon in her crack, and comes back down beside him. The boy is staring at her. "She's never gone up before," he says.

events.name: The Second Night
events.intro: The second night. The ruts lead off the road into an old orchard, and there, between the trees, is a light. A shed with its doors propped open, a generator coughing, and inside, on a cart, a machine: glass tubes, brass, a chair with straps sized for something small. A row of cages along the wall. In every cage, a Nincada, very quiet. The boy's hand is white on his sword. "This is it," he breathes. "This is where." The Shedinja above his shoulder has gone completely still.

success.text: You creep to the window. On the bench, a notebook: page after page of numbers, and dates, and words like "forced", "accelerated", "unrecoverable". At the bottom of the last page, a name and an address in the next town, where the cart goes tomorrow night. You take a photo. The boy reads the word unrecoverable over your shoulder and does not say anything for a long time.

He is already halfway out of the trees, sword up, when you catch his arm. "Not now," you whisper. "Not alone, not angry." He fights you for a second. Then the Shedinja drifts down between you and him, and he stops. "Tomorrow," he says, shaking. "Tomorrow night. With you." Inside, the generator coughs, and a Nincada in a cage scratches once at the bars.

events.name: The Third Night
events.intro: The third night. The cart, the machine, and beside it a man in a white coat with the badge of the evil team on the pocket, checking dials. He looks up and sees the boy, and the Shedinja, and his face lights up, not with fear but with interest. "Oh! Subject eleven. Still stable, I see. Remarkable." He steps in front of his machine. "I can't let you break it. Do you know how long it took to get right?" Behind him, three Ninjask rise off the cart, buzzing, very fast.

success.text: The boy draws his sword. The Shedinja does not move from his shoulder. The machine hums.

choices.label: Ask him to change her back.

success.text: "Can you undo it?" you ask. He actually thinks about it, head on one side. "No," he says. "That's rather the point." The boy makes a sound you will not forget. Then he swings his sword, not at the man, at the machine: glass, brass, every tube. The scientist shouts and runs into the dark, his Ninjask streaming after him. The cages spring open. Nobody chases him. There is nothing left to chase him for.

events.name: Dawn

remembers.notice: She knows what to do. She drifts from cage to cage, and the frightened Nincada come out one by one and gather under her, like children under a lamp. She stays a Shedinja. She is not sad about it. The boy watches her and, for the first time, he smiles at her instead of at the road.

events.intro: The sun comes up over a broken machine and a shed full of open cages. The Nincada are coming out, blinking, one by one. The boy sits on the cart with the sword across his knees. The Shedinja hangs beside him. She has not changed. She will not change. He knows that now. "I thought when I found them, I'd get her back," he says. "I didn't. But nobody else will be made like her. That's something." He looks at the sword. "I don't need this any more." One of the Nincada has walked all the way across the floor and sat down on your boot.

success.text: He holds it out flat across both hands, the way you hand over something that matters. It is light, and sharp, and the tape on the sheath is his. "It likes bugs," he says, and nearly laughs. The Nincada on your boot climbs up your leg and into your arms. The boy walks off down the road in the morning light, not hunting any more, with his sister a little above his shoulder, exactly where she always is.

effects.text: You hunted the one who made a girl into a Shedinja. Nobody else will be made like her.

success.text: "Keep it," you say. "Not for hunting. For remembering." He looks at it for a long time and then slides it home in its taped sheath. The Nincada on your boot climbs into your arms. The boy walks off down the road in the morning light, his sister a little above his shoulder. Once, before the bend, he turns round and waves, and so, in her way, does she.

effects.text: You hunted the one who made a girl into a Shedinja. Nobody else will be made like her.

events.name: The Fake Family

remembers.notice: The father's eyes keep sliding to a car parked across the road: long, gold-trimmed, with a ring of gilt on its door. The Gilt Circle's mark. He writes something in a tiny notebook and puts it away before anyone sees. You see.

events.intro: A school entrance on enrolment day: gates, flowers, nervous parents. One family stands a little apart. A father in a perfect suit, smiling a perfect smile. A mother, very beautiful, very still, holding her handbag the way you would hold something you might need to throw. And between them a small girl with enormous eyes and an Espurr in her arms. All three of them are lying about something. You can tell, the way you can tell when a room has been tidied in a hurry. The girl tugs your sleeve and whispers, "Papa's a spy. Mama's scary. I can hear what people think. Don't tell them." Her Espurr stares at you without blinking, for a very long time.

success.text: Her face goes bright as a lamp. She holds out her fist, and in it, warm and a bit sticky, is her spare Poké Doll. "For keeping secrets," she whispers. "It's my best one." Her mother glances down at you both, sharp as a pin, and then away. The girl is beaming. "Will you come to the interview? We need a family friend. I picked you."

choices.label: Help them get into the school.

success.text: The father turns his perfect smile on you. "How kind. Our references fell through. Family friend?" The mother says nothing and looks at you as if measuring you for a coat. The girl squeezes your hand. "The interview's soon," the father says. "Do you lie well?" It is clearly a joke. It is clearly not a joke.

The girl looks at her parents, then pulls you down to whisper. "Papa's looking for a man who buys old buildings. I heard him think the word warehouse, and the word Thursday, and a number, nine." She bites her lip. "Mama thinks it about the same man. But angrier." The Espurr's ears twitch. "Come to the interview," she says. "We need a family friend. Then you can see."

events.name: The Interview
events.intro: A headmaster's office: tall windows, a clock that ticks too loudly, a headmaster with half-moon glasses. You sit at the end of the row as the family friend. The girl is swinging her legs. The headmaster turns to the father first. "And what is your line of work, sir?" The father's smile does not move. Under the desk, his foot taps once. He has not prepared for this question. He has prepared for every other question in the world.

success.text: "Paper," you say, before he can. "He's in paper. Very boring. He tells us about it at dinner." The father takes it like a relay baton. "Envelopes, mostly. Some card." The headmaster nods, bored already, and writes down paper. The father does not look at you. His foot stops tapping.

failure.text: "Paper," you say, and your voice cracks halfway through. The headmaster looks up. The father rescues it smoothly: "Paper, yes. Our friend is shy." The headmaster writes paper, frowning slightly. You go hot to the ears. The girl pats your knee.

success.text: "He works very hard," you say. "He's always away. She misses him." The girl nods fiercely. The headmaster softens and writes something kind. The father looks at you for one long second, and something in his perfect smile goes, briefly, real.

events.name: The Interview: Mama
events.intro: The headmaster turns to the mother. "And your hobbies, madam?" She smiles beautifully. "Gardening." The headmaster brightens. "Oh, what do you grow?" A pause. A very small, very dangerous pause. Her hand tightens on her handbag. You get the strong sense she has never grown anything, and that the last thing she pruned was a person.

success.text: "Roses," you say. "She has a terrible time with greenfly. She takes it very personally." The mother turns her beautiful head and looks at you with something like gratitude. "Very personally," she agrees. "I do not let them win." The headmaster laughs, delighted, and writes roses.

failure.text: "Roses," you say, but it comes out as a question. The mother finishes it herself, smoothly. "Roses. And some herbs." Then, quietly, to you, as the headmaster writes: "You blinked." You will think about that for days.

success.text: "She's very protective," you say. "Of the family." The mother looks at you, startled, and then, quite slowly, she nods. "Yes," she says. "That is my hobby." The headmaster laughs, thinking it is a joke, and writes family.

events.name: The Interview: The Girl
events.intro: Last, the headmaster smiles at the girl. "And is there anything special about you, young lady?" She opens her mouth. You can see the truth climbing up into it: I can hear what you're thinking, you're thinking about lunch. Her parents go rigid. The Espurr in her lap stares at the headmaster without blinking. The clock ticks. She looks at you.

success.text: You catch her eye and tap the side of your nose. She swallows the truth whole. "I'm very good at guessing," she says, sweetly. "Like, I bet you're thinking about lunch." The headmaster laughs so hard his glasses fall off. "Accepted," he says, wiping his eyes. "Goodness. Accepted." Outside the office the father shakes your hand, and the mother nods, and the girl hugs your legs. "Same time in a while?" the father murmurs. "There's one more thing we have to do."

failure.text: You try to signal her, and she misreads it completely. "I can hear what people think," she says, brightly. Her parents freeze. The headmaster beams. "What an imagination! Accepted." Outside, the mother breathes out through her nose for a long time. "Children," says the father. "One more thing to do, in a while. Will you come?"

success.text: "I can hear what people think," she says. The headmaster chuckles. "Can you? What am I thinking?" "Lunch," she says. "And that your mum never came to your interview." The room goes very quiet. The headmaster takes his glasses off. "Accepted," he says, gently, after a while. Outside, her parents hold her between them. "One more thing to do," the father says to you. "In a while. Will you come?"

events.name: What Papa Found

remembers.notice: The father finally says it out loud. "The Gilt Circle. I have been inside their accounts for a year. They buy old buildings and fill them with stolen Pokémon." Warehouse. Thursday. Nine: the words the girl whispered at the school gate. It is Thursday. The girl looks up at you, very pleased. "I told you it was a secret about them."

addChoices.label: Tell Papa what she told you.

success.text: You tell him: warehouse nine, tonight. He goes still. Then he looks at his daughter, and at you, and laughs, properly, for the first time. "We've been watching the wrong door for a month." The team's plan goes nowhere: by the time they arrive, the police are already inside, and the father is in a café across the road, drinking cocoa with his family. The Espurr hops into your lap. "It wants to come with you," the girl says. "It told me."

effects.text: A pretend family let you be their friend, and you helped stop a team's plan with a secret a child heard.

remembers.notice: The father finally says it out loud. "The Gilt Circle. I have been inside their accounts for a year. They buy old buildings and fill them with stolen Pokémon to sell." The mother checks something in her handbag. "Tonight," she says, "they lose the building."

Warehouse. Thursday. Nine. The words the girl whispered at the school gate. It is Thursday. The warehouse is number nine. The girl looks up at you, very pleased. "I told you it was a secret about them."

events.intro: A warehouse district, after dark. The father has changed into a dark coat; the mother has not changed at all, which is somehow more frightening. The girl has insisted on coming and holds your hand. The father points to a big building with a padlock and a lamp. "The evil team keeps stolen Pokémon there, to sell. Tonight they move them." He hesitates, a real hesitation. "I should not have brought her. But she would have heard me think about it anyway." Out of the shadows step four grunts, all men, all large.

success.text: The father moves like smoke. The mother moves like a closing door. You take the two in front.

win.text: A pretend family let you be their friend, and you helped them empty a warehouse of stolen Pokémon.

lose.text: A pretend family let you be their friend. The mother finished the fight you started.

success.text: You keep her behind you while her parents do whatever it is they do. It is very fast and very quiet and you do not see much of it. She does not watch either. She is busy telling you what everyone is thinking, in a whisper: the grunts are thinking ow. When it is over the doors are open and the Pokémon are walking out free. Her Espurr hops from her arms into yours. "It wants to come with you," she says. "It told me. It thinks you're a good friend. For a pretend one."

effects.text: A pretend family let you be their friend, and you kept the girl safe while they emptied a warehouse.

events.name: The Stand

remembers.notice: Your Ghost-type, the one closest to you, drifts forward. The Dusclops drifts forward. They stop a hand apart and look at each other with the long, unhurried look of two things that have both been somewhere nobody else has. The delinquent sees it. His mouth falls open. "It's never looked at anyone like that," he says. "Not since him."

success.text: They do not make a sound. They do not need to. After a while the Dusclops turns its one red eye on the delinquent, and then it does something it has never done: it puts its big grey hand on his shoulder, the way an old man would. He takes his sunglasses off. He does not say anything for a long time. Then: "Thanks. I didn't know it could still do that."

events.intro: Under a railway bridge, a delinquent leans on the wall with his arms folded: long coat, dark glasses, and a pompadour so enormous it has its own weather. Behind him floats a Dusclops. When he shifts his weight, it shifts. When he cracks his knuckles, it cracks its knuckles, a beat late, gently, like an echo. He sees you looking past him and goes stiff. "You can see it? Nobody can see it." He pushes off the wall. "It showed up when my grandad died. It punches people for me." The Dusclops does not punch anyone. It is not looking at you at all. It is looking at {lead}, very steadily, with its one red eye.

success.text: "Fine. You asked for it." He throws out his Poké Balls. Behind him, the Dusclops does not move. When he points at {lead} and shouts, it turns its head away.

He goes quiet. All the swagger drains out of him at once, and he is just a kid under a lot of hair. "It was his," he says. "It stayed." He takes off his sunglasses. His eyes are red round the edges. "He used to do my hair. Every morning. Took ages." Behind him the Dusclops lifts one hand, slowly, and smooths the side of the pompadour, and he lets it.

He opens his mouth to argue. Nothing comes out. He looks over his shoulder at the Dusclops, and it looks back at him, patient as a grandfather. "...No," he says at last, very quietly. "It stops me." He sits down on the kerb. "Every time I go to swing at someone, it grabs my arm. I tell everyone it's the other way round. Sounds better."

events.name: The One Behind You
events.intro: As you turn to go, something small comes out from behind the Dusclops's back, where it must have been hiding all along: a Duskull, round and grey, with a single red light for an eye. It floats straight past the delinquent, past you, and takes up position just behind {lead}'s shoulder, a little above, exactly the way the Dusclops stands behind him. It folds its arms. The delinquent laughs, a real laugh. "Grandad's old one had a little one. Looks like it picked you." He puts his glasses back on. "Maybe I'll do something with this. Channel it. Help people see their own."

success.text: It stays where it is. When {lead} moves, it moves, a beat late, gently. You feel steadier with it there, the way you feel steadier with your back to a wall. The delinquent salutes you with two fingers, pompadour first, and walks off under the bridge with his grandad's ghost at his back.

effects.text: A delinquent's grandfather stood behind him as a Dusclops. A little Duskull chose to stand behind yours.

choices.label: Tell it to stay with him.

success.text: "He needs it more," you say. The Duskull looks at you, at the delinquent, and floats back to him, and settles behind his other shoulder, opposite the Dusclops. He stands there with a ghost on either side, trying very hard not to cry. "Two of them," he says. "Grandad, you show-off." He waves you off with two fingers.

events.name: The Magical Bakery
events.intro: A little bakery on the corner, with a striped awning and a bell over the door. Inside, the cream has got up and is walking about: small soft blobs of it, wandering across the counter, climbing the cake stands, peering into the till. They are Milcery, a dozen of them, and they smell of vanilla. Behind the counter a baker girl in a flour-covered apron claps her hands. "When I spin, I transform! So does the cream!" Her Milcery spins on the counter. So does she, round and round, in a cloud of flour, and when it settles she is in a frilly apron with ribbons on it and is holding a whisk like a sword. She points it at the back door. "A sugar monster ate the shop's sugar. All of it. Help me?" From the back room comes a long, enormous, satisfied burp.

success.text: You spin. You feel ridiculous for exactly one turn, and then you do not, because {lead} is spinning too, and the flour is glittering, and when you stop you are both, somehow, sparkling. "TRANSFORMED!" the baker shouts. You charge the back room together. Inside is a Gulpin so large it fills the doorway, with sugar on its face.

You do not spin. The baker looks a little disappointed, but follows you into the back room with her whisk up. The sugar monster is a Gulpin, but a very large one: it fills the doorway, and it has sugar on its face, and it is not sorry.

You put your head round the back door. The sugar monster is a Gulpin, a very large one, sitting in a pile of empty sacks. It looks at you with sugar on its face and, slowly, its huge mouth wobbles. It is not a monster. It is starving. Through the back window you can see why: where there should be a garden, there is a car park, new and grey. "There was a berry patch there," the baker whispers. "Before they paved it."

events.name: The Paved Patch
events.intro: The Gulpin follows you out to the car park and stands where its patch used to be, looking at the tarmac. It puts one stubby arm on the ground, as if feeling for roots. The baker stands beside it with her whisk hanging down. "It used to come to the back door every morning," she says. "I gave it the broken biscuits. I thought it just stopped coming." There is one bare strip of earth left at the edge, by the bins.

success.text: You dig the strip with your hands and the baker's cake slice. You plant the best berry you have. You water it with the bakery's watering can, the one shaped like a teapot. The Gulpin watches every second. By evening a green shoot is up, and the Gulpin is sitting beside it, guarding it, not eating anything. "It can be the taster," the baker says. "It eats one of everything and tells me if it's good." The Gulpin, solemnly, burps yes.
You are sorry for it. The sugar is still gone. The Gulpin seems to understand that, and squares up, sad and enormous, in the middle of the car park.

events.name: The Flavour of Your Choice

remembers.notice: Through the back window you can see the Gulpin, sitting by its green shoot with a crumb on its lip, wearing a paper hat that says TASTER.

events.intro: The bakery is quiet again. The baker has spun back into her floury apron and is counting what is left. One of the Milcery has not wandered off with the others. It has climbed up your sleeve and is sitting on your shoulder, smelling of vanilla, wobbling. "Oh," the baker says. "It's chosen you. They do that." She takes down a jar of something pink. "When it grows up, it becomes whatever you dream for it. What flavour?"

success.text: "Classic," she says approvingly. She gives you a little Strawberry Sweet in a paper twist. "For when it's ready." The Milcery wobbles happily. It already smells of vanilla, and it plans to keep it that way.

effects.text: A baker spun, and so did the cream. Your Milcery chose vanilla cream.
